title: IF OBEDIENCE PROVES YOU’RE SAVED… WHY DID JESUS SAVE A THIEF WHO COULDN’T OBEY ANOTHER COMMAND?
paragraphs: IF OBEDIENCE PROVES YOU’RE SAVED… WHY DID JESUS SAVE A THIEF WHO COULDN’T OBEY ANOTHER COMMAND?

The terrifying difference between following Jesus because you are saved and trying to obey Him so He will save you. One leads to freedom. The other can leave you religious, exhausted, and dangerously far from grace.
There was a man dying beside Jesus who had no time left to become a better Christian.
No time to attend church.
No time to be baptized.
No time to give an offering, repair his reputation, restore everything he had stolen, or build a beautiful testimony of years spent faithfully serving God.
His hands were nailed to a cross.
His past was stained.
His future, humanly speaking, was finished.
And yet, before the sun went down, Jesus promised him paradise.
If obedience is evidence of salvation, what evidence did that dying criminal have?
And if obedience doesn't matter, why did Jesus repeatedly command His followers to obey Him?
Because somewhere between the cross of Christ and the expectations of religious people, a dangerous confusion has entered the church.
Some believers are terrified that one more failure will make God abandon them.
Others are so comfortable talking about grace that they have stopped taking sin seriously.
One group lives as though Jesus didn't finish enough.
The other lives as though His sacrifice didn't cost anything.
And somewhere in the middle stands a bloodstained Savior who refuses to let us turn either obedience or grace into something He never intended.
This is not merely a theological argument.
This is about the woman who cried last night because she promised God she would never fall into that sin again.
It's about the man who has attended church for twenty years, faithfully serves in ministry, and secretly wonders whether God loves him or merely tolerates him.
It's about the young believer who genuinely wants to follow Jesus but feels crushed by Christians who seem more interested in measuring his failures than helping him grow.
And it's about the person who keeps saying, "God knows my heart," while deliberately protecting the very sin Christ is calling him to surrender.
All four need the Gospel.
Not a softer Gospel.
Not a harsher Gospel.
The real Gospel.
Because the question isn't simply whether Christians should obey.
The question is whether our obedience is the fruit of salvation, the price of salvation, or a counterfeit we have mistaken for salvation itself.
And Scripture answers that question with extraordinary clarity.
Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9:
The Greek word translated "grace" is χάρις (charis), commonly referring to grace, favor, or gift. In this passage, God's saving grace is not presented as wages earned by religious performance.
It is a gift.
And a gift ceases to be a gift when we imagine we can purchase it with enough moral improvement.
Notice the order.
Grace.
Faith.
Salvation.
Not obedience first, then acceptance.
Not perfection first, then forgiveness.
Not religious achievement first, then eternal life.
God saves sinners through Jesus Christ, not through their successful attempts to become worthy of Him.
But something remarkable happens when we keep reading.
Ephesians 2:10 says:
"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."
Did you see it?
The very passage that declares we are not saved by works also declares that we are saved for good works.
The Greek word ποίημα (poiēma), translated "workmanship," describes something made or produced. Believers are God's workmanship, created anew in Christ.
And the Greek expression ἐπὶ ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς (epi ergois agathois) points to the good works for which this new creation is intended.
In other words, obedience does not manufacture the new birth.
It belongs to the life that flows from it.
We are not saved because we obey. We are called to obey because God has saved us.
That difference is not a theological technicality.
It is the difference between a child obeying because he belongs to a loving father and an orphan desperately working to earn a place at the family table.
And some of you have been living like spiritual orphans for years.
You pray, but not always because you delight in speaking with God.
Sometimes you pray because you're frightened that missing a day will make Him angry.
You read Scripture, but not always because you hunger for His truth.
Sometimes you read because you imagine your spiritual worth depends on completing a religious checklist.
You serve, give, fast, and attend church.
And none of those things is wrong.
They can be beautiful expressions of genuine faith.
But somewhere along the journey, your heart quietly exchanged intimacy for performance.
You stopped asking, "Lord, how can I love You more?"
And started asking, "Lord, have I done enough for You to love me?"
Listen carefully.
If Jesus had waited until you were worthy of His love, Calvary would never have happened.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we achieved spiritual consistency.
Not after we learned how to look holy in front of other Christians.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is grace.
But grace has been terribly misunderstood by some people who want the comfort of forgiveness without the inconvenience of surrender.
And that brings us to the other side of this conversation.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments."
The Greek text reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
A faithful rendering is:
"If you love me, you will keep my commandments."
The verb τηρήσετε (tērēsete) is future indicative, describing what those who love Jesus will do. The statement connects love for Christ with obedience to His commands.
Jesus was not describing a relationship in which our works purchase His affection.
He was describing the natural expression of genuine love.
Think about it.

If someone repeatedly tells you they love you while knowingly betraying you, dismissing your words, and refusing every invitation to change, eventually you begin questioning what that person means by love.
Not because love requires flawless performance.
But because real love cannot remain permanently indifferent to the beloved.
The same principle confronts our relationship with Jesus.
A person may stumble while sincerely loving Christ.
A believer may struggle for years against a deeply rooted sin.
A wounded Christian may experience seasons of spiritual exhaustion, confusion, and painful weakness.
But there is a difference between fighting sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and declaring that repentance is unnecessary.
There is a difference between saying, "Lord, help me overcome this," and saying, "Lord, accept this because I have no intention of changing."
Grace does not make rebellion holy.
Grace calls rebels home.
Paul confronts this directly in Romans 6:1–2:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid."
The Greek response begins:
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It is a forceful rejection, often rendered "By no means!" or "Absolutely not!"
Paul is not entertaining the idea that God's forgiveness gives Christians permission to embrace sin.
He rejects it.
Why?
Because union with Christ changes our relationship to sin.
The believer has not merely received a religious pardon while remaining untouched by the Savior.
The believer has been brought into a new relationship with the crucified and risen Christ.
That is why repentance matters.
That is why holiness matters.
That is why obedience matters.
Not because Jesus needs our performance to complete His sacrifice.
But because the One who died to rescue us from sin did not die so that we could celebrate remaining enslaved to it.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not the enemy of holiness.
Grace is the very power that teaches us to pursue it.
And yet, here is where many sincere Christians are wounded.
They hear the word "obedience," and immediately remember the religious environment that nearly destroyed them.
A church where every mistake became public humiliation.
A family where spiritual maturity was measured by appearances.
A ministry where questions were treated as rebellion.
A community where people were quick to condemn visible sins while quietly excusing pride, greed, cruelty, and hypocrisy.
They were taught that a faithful Christian never struggles.
Never doubts.
Never feels depressed.
Never admits weakness.
Never needs help.
And when their humanity eventually became impossible to hide, they were made to feel as though they had disappointed God beyond repair.
Some stopped praying.
Some stopped attending church.
Some began hiding their struggles behind carefully rehearsed smiles.
And some walked away from Christianity altogether, believing that the merciless religion they experienced accurately represented Jesus Christ.
But consider the Savior revealed in Scripture.
Jesus did not approve of sin.
He also did not treat broken sinners as disposable.
In John 8:11, within the traditional account of the woman caught in adultery, Jesus says:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
Both parts matter.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy and a call to change.
Compassion and holiness.
Grace and truth.

A textual note is important here: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked or bracketed in many modern Bibles. The account should therefore be handled with appropriate textual caution. Nevertheless, the combination of mercy toward sinners and a call to repentance is firmly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus did not tell sinners that their sins were imaginary.
Neither did He teach that their sins placed them beyond the reach of His mercy.
And we must not separate what Christ holds together.
When churches preach holiness without grace, they can produce fear, hypocrisy, and despair.
When churches preach grace without repentance, they can produce complacency and spiritual self-deception.
But when churches faithfully proclaim Jesus Christ, they call sinners to repentance while pointing them toward the mercy and transforming power found in Him.
Now return to the criminal on the cross.
Luke 23 records two criminals crucified alongside Jesus.
One mocked Him.
The other acknowledged their guilt and the innocence of Christ.
Then he turned toward the dying Savior and pleaded:
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." (Luke 23:42, KJV)
The Greek text preserves the heart of his request:
μνήσθητί μου (mnēsthēti mou).
"Remember me."
Two words.
No impressive testimony.
No long history of religious service.
No opportunity to prove himself through years of obedience.
Just a guilty man turning toward Jesus in faith.
And Jesus answered:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." (Luke 23:43, KJV)
The Greek includes:
σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
"Today you will be with me in paradise."
The promise centers on being with Jesus.
Not on the criminal's religious achievements.
Not on his ability to compensate for his crimes.
Not on a future opportunity to accumulate good works.
Christ Himself was his hope.
But we should not overlook something extraordinary.
Although the criminal could not demonstrate a lifetime of obedience, his response was not spiritually empty.
He acknowledged his guilt.
He recognized Jesus' innocence.
He rebuked the other criminal.
He appealed to Jesus as the One whose kingdom extended beyond their approaching deaths.
These were meaningful expressions of faith and repentance.
His actions did not purchase salvation.
They revealed the direction of a heart turning toward Christ.
The thief was not saved by a record of good works.
Yet his faith was not indifferent to truth.
That is the distinction we must understand.
The absence of time for a lifetime of obedience is not the same as the absence of a changed response to Jesus.
The dying criminal teaches us that salvation rests on Christ, not accumulated religious merit.
He does not teach us that someone who has years to follow Jesus may deliberately reject His lordship without concern.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of this account is that the criminal who received paradise had no opportunity to build the kind of Christian résumé that impresses religious people.
But he had Jesus.
And Jesus was enough.
Now imagine that same dying man somehow being taken down from the cross, miraculously healed, and given another thirty years to live.
Would we expect him to return to his former life with complete indifference toward the Savior who rescued him?
Would we imagine that genuine gratitude for Christ would have no effect on his choices?
Of course not.
His obedience would not be payment for paradise.
It would be a response to mercy.
And that is where James enters the conversation.
James 2:17 says:
"Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone."
James is not contradicting Paul.
Paul rejects works as the basis of justification before God.
James challenges the claim that a merely verbal profession, disconnected from any meaningful response to God, constitutes living faith.
James asks us to consider the difference between saying we believe and possessing a faith that actually moves us.
The Greek phrase πίστις νεκρά (pistis nekra) means "dead faith."
A faith that exists only as an empty claim is not the vibrant trust in Christ that Scripture commends.
And this should make us examine ourselves.
Not obsessively count every failure.
Not compare our spiritual progress with everyone else's.
Not assume that every painful struggle proves we are unsaved.
But honestly ask whether our profession of faith is shaping the direction of our lives.
Are we becoming more willing to confess our sins?
More willing to forgive?
More willing to speak truthfully?
More willing to resist what dishonors Christ?
More willing to love people who cannot repay us?
More willing to admit when we are wrong?
More willing to surrender the parts of our lives we once insisted God could never touch?
Spiritual growth is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like a man finally apologizing to his wife without blaming her for his behavior.
Sometimes it looks like a young woman refusing to return to a destructive relationship, even while crying because leaving hurts.
Sometimes it looks like someone quietly closing a browser window and choosing to pray instead.
Sometimes it looks like a believer confessing an addiction and asking for help rather than pretending the struggle does not exist.
Sometimes it looks like returning to Scripture after months of spiritual numbness.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it looks like a Christian saying, "I was wrong," without adding excuses.
And sometimes obedience is simply getting up after another failure, turning back toward Christ, and refusing to call sin your home.
None of those actions earns the love of God.
But they can reflect the transforming work of His grace.
And no, this does not mean every believer grows at the same speed.
Jesus' parable of the soils in Matthew 13 reminds us that spiritual responses differ.
Paul's letters reveal churches filled with real believers who still needed serious correction.
The New Testament repeatedly calls Christians to grow, repent, persevere, and mature.
That would make little sense if conversion immediately removed every weakness.
Sanctification is not the claim that Christians never stumble.
It is God's ongoing work of making His people more like Christ.
And that work can be painful.
Especially when the Holy Spirit begins confronting sins we have spent years defending.
But here is a truth that deserves to be written across the walls of every church where wounded believers are afraid to confess their struggles.
Conviction invites you to return to Christ. Condemnation tells you there is no hope in returning.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
In the Greek, the central declaration is:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
"So then, there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus."
The word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation or an adverse judicial sentence.
Paul's declaration is not that sin becomes harmless.
It is that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemnation from which He has delivered them.
That freedom does not make holiness unnecessary.
Read the rest of Romans 8.
Paul describes life in the Spirit, the putting to death of sinful deeds, adoption as God's children, suffering, hope, and the inseparable love of God in Christ.
No condemnation is the beginning of a Spirit-led life.
Not permission to abandon it.
And perhaps this is exactly what someone reading needs to hear.
You have been measuring God's love by the quality of your most recent week.
When you prayed consistently, you felt accepted.
When you resisted temptation, you felt secure.
When you failed, you imagined heaven closing its doors.
You confessed the same sin again and wondered whether Jesus had finally grown tired of hearing your voice.
You looked at Christians who seemed stronger and wondered why transformation appeared easier for everyone else.
But your assurance cannot rest on the illusion that you will never struggle again.
It must rest on the faithful Savior who died and rose again, whose promises call you to trust Him and whose Spirit leads His people into holiness.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice whose faithfulness is emphasized.
His.
Not the perfection of your confession.
Not the eloquence of your prayer.
Not the intensity of your tears.
His faithfulness.
That does not make repentance a meaningless ritual.
Genuine confession agrees with God about sin and turns toward His mercy.
But the hope of forgiveness is grounded in the character and saving work of God.
So when you fall, do not run from the only One who can restore you.
Run to Him.
Confess honestly.
Seek help when needed.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Remove opportunities for repeated temptation.
Receive the correction of Scripture.
Keep walking in the light.
And when someone tries to convince you that grace means you should never feel concerned about deliberate, ongoing rebellion, remember that Scripture speaks differently.
First John 2:3 says:
"And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments."
That verse should not be twisted into a demand for sinless perfection.
John himself has already acknowledged that believers need forgiveness.
But it should not be emptied of its meaning either.
Our relationship with Jesus has moral consequences.
A profession of faith that persistently rejects His commands deserves serious examination.
Not because human obedience can replace the cross.
But because saving faith does not regard the Savior's authority as irrelevant.
And this is where legalism must be named accurately.
Legalism is not simply taking obedience seriously.
A Christian is not automatically legalistic because he believes sexual purity matters, dishonesty is sinful, repentance is necessary, or Jesus' commands should be followed.
Jesus Himself called His disciples to costly obedience.
The apostles taught holiness.
The New Testament contains numerous moral commands.
Calling people to obey Scripture is not inherently legalism.

Legalism appears when we make human obedience the basis of our acceptance before God, impose human rules as though they were divine commands, or elevate outward religious performance while neglecting the deeper demands of faith, mercy, and love.
It can also appear when people use their apparent righteousness to despise others.
Remember the Pharisee and the tax collector in Luke 18?
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
He pointed to his fasting and giving.
The tax collector stood at a distance, acknowledged his sin, and pleaded for mercy.
Jesus said the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
The problem was not that fasting and giving were inherently wrong.
The problem was a self-righteous heart trusting in its own religious superiority.
And that danger has not disappeared.
It still walks into churches carrying Bibles.
It still speaks confidently about holiness.
It still notices everyone else's failures while carefully protecting its own.
It still mistakes being stricter than other Christians for being closer to Jesus.
It can even turn good biblical practices into trophies of spiritual superiority.
But the cross leaves no room for boasting in ourselves.
At Calvary, every believer stands as someone who needed mercy.
The pastor.
The worship leader.
The new convert.
The person recovering from addiction.
The faithful grandmother.
The former criminal.
The person who grew up in church.
The person who arrived yesterday.
Every one of us needs the same Savior.
And the ground at the foot of the cross is no place for pretending we rescued ourselves.
There is another uncomfortable truth we must face.
Some Christians are so afraid of legalism that they hesitate to call anyone to repentance.
They fear that confronting sin will sound judgmental.
They worry that preaching holiness will drive people away.
They have watched religious abuse hurt people and sincerely want to avoid repeating it.
That concern can come from genuine compassion.
But withholding what Jesus actually taught is not the answer.
A doctor who refuses to discuss a serious illness because the patient might become upset is not necessarily showing kindness.
Likewise, a church that never speaks about repentance may leave people comfortable in spiritual danger.
Love tells the truth.
But love also cares how that truth is delivered.
Galatians 6:1 calls spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in wrongdoing with gentleness, while watching themselves.
Restoration.
Gentleness.
Humility.
Those words belong together.
Biblical correction is not an opportunity to humiliate someone.
It is an act intended to help restore them.
If our correction delights in exposing another person's shame, something is wrong with our hearts.
If our preaching produces admiration for our own strictness rather than reverence for Christ, something is wrong with our emphasis.
And if our version of holiness makes struggling people afraid to tell the truth, we should examine whether we have represented the gentleness of Jesus faithfully.
Christ is holy.
Christ is merciful.
Christ is truthful.
Christ is compassionate.
We do not honor Him by sacrificing one part of His character to defend another.
So what does real obedience look like?
It looks like loving Jesus enough to take His words seriously.
It looks like repentance that begins in the heart and becomes visible in the life.
It looks like faith working through love, as Galatians 5:6 teaches.
It looks like dependence on the Holy Spirit rather than confidence in human strength.
It looks like a willingness to obey even when obedience costs something.
It looks like humility when corrected.
It looks like gratitude rather than spiritual entitlement.
It looks like refusing to use grace as an excuse for sin.
And it looks like refusing to use obedience as a weapon against those who are still growing.
Most importantly, it keeps returning to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about becoming impressive at religious behavior.
It is about being reconciled to God through His Son and being transformed into His likeness.
Jesus did not come merely to produce better-behaved people who could congratulate themselves on their moral accomplishments.
He came to save sinners.
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
He calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
And those who belong to Him are called to follow Him.
Not to improve upon His finished sacrifice.
But because His sacrifice has changed everything.
That is why Philippians 2:12–13 is so beautiful.

Paul urges believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, then immediately explains that God is at work in them, producing both the willing and the doing according to His good pleasure.
He does not say to work for salvation as though Christ had left the payment unfinished.
He speaks of living out the salvation God is working within His people.
God's grace does not make our participation meaningless.
Our participation does not make God's grace unnecessary.
We obey because God is at work in us.
And even our growth becomes a reason to praise Him.
Now, before you move on, I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question for the person sitting beside you.
Not a question for the Christian you secretly think needs this article.
A question for you.
Are you using obedience to earn a love Jesus already demonstrated at the cross?
Or are you using grace to excuse a sin He is calling you to surrender?
Perhaps you have been living in the first prison.
You are exhausted.
You love Jesus, but you constantly feel like a disappointment.
You believe the Gospel is true for other people, yet struggle to believe His mercy can reach your repeated failures.
You have mistaken spiritual growth for never needing forgiveness again.
Hear this.
The answer is not to stop pursuing holiness.
The answer is to stop treating holiness as the purchase price of God's grace.
Come back to Christ.
Let His love produce obedience rather than allowing fear to counterfeit it.
Or perhaps you have been living in the second prison.
You know what Scripture says.
You know the habit is destroying you.
You know the relationship is drawing you away from Christ.
You know the bitterness has hardened your heart.
You know the dishonesty must end.
But you have convinced yourself that because salvation is by grace, surrender can wait indefinitely.
Hear this too.
The answer is not to abandon grace.
The answer is to receive grace for what Scripture says it is: God's saving favor that also trains and transforms His people.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval of sin.
Do not treat the wounds of Christ as permission to remain in what He died to redeem.
Today is a good day to repent.
Not because Jesus is reluctant to receive you.
But because He is worthy of your surrender.
And if you have spent years swinging between fear and compromise, perhaps today is the day to stop looking at yourself as the center of the story.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the crown of thorns.
Look at the nails.
Look at the innocent Son of God bearing the sins of the guilty.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the risen Savior who calls His sheep to hear His voice and follow Him.
There is your hope.
Not your flawless record.
Not your religious reputation.
Not your ability to impress other believers.
Christ.
Always Christ.
And the closer you draw to Him, the less attractive both self-righteousness and careless rebellion should become.
Because genuine grace humbles the proud and gives hope to the broken.
It tells the religious performer, "You cannot save yourself."
It tells the careless sinner, "You cannot make peace with what Christ calls you to leave behind."
It tells the repentant believer, "Keep following Jesus."
And it tells the exhausted Christian, "Your Savior is greater than your weakness."
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Not that sin was insignificant.
But that Jesus was willing to bear its terrible cost.
Not that obedience is irrelevant.
But that obedience finds its rightful place as the grateful response of a redeemed life.
Not that Christians become perfect overnight.
But that the One who begins a good work in His people is faithful to carry it forward, as Philippians 1:6 assures us.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a phrase.
Think of Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He denied Jesus three times.
He wept bitterly.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's denial was not harmless.
His restoration was not cheap.
But his worst failure was not the final chapter of his life.
Think of Paul.
A persecutor of Christians.
A man whose former actions caused suffering among the very people he later served.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him, and the persecutor became a preacher of the Gospel.
Paul did not earn that calling by being a good man beforehand.
He received mercy.
And that mercy transformed the direction of his life.
Think of the criminal on the cross.
His story ended in earthly shame.
Yet Christ promised him paradise.
Three men.
Three different histories.
Three powerful reminders that Jesus Christ is able to save sinners.
But notice something.
Peter was restored to faithful service.
Paul's life was redirected toward Christ.
The dying criminal turned to Jesus with the little time he had remaining.
Different circumstances.
The same saving Savior.
And faith was never presented as a license to despise the One who saved them.
This is the message a hurting generation needs.
Not a Christianity that makes people terrified of admitting weakness.
Not a Christianity that congratulates people for remaining in rebellion.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ, who receives repentant sinners and calls them into a new life.
A Savior holy enough to confront our sin.
Merciful enough to forgive it.
Powerful enough to transform us.
And faithful enough to sustain those who belong to Him.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to pretend.
You can begin with an honest prayer.

"Lord Jesus, I have tried to earn what only Your grace can give. Or I have used Your grace to excuse what You are calling me to surrender. Forgive me. Teach me to trust Your finished work, turn from my sin, and follow You through the power of Your Spirit. Make my obedience an expression of love, not a performance driven by fear. Keep my eyes on You. Amen."
You do not need to expose private details to strangers to be honest about needing God's help.
And if God has been restoring you from a season of spiritual failure, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Not to prove your spirituality to anyone.
But because sometimes an honest confession of our need for grace becomes the encouragement another wounded believer has been praying to find.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
We want this community to become a place where people are not simply moved by a message for a moment, but are continually directed back to the Word of God and the Savior it reveals.
That is also why I want to invite you to consider something deeper than reading, reacting, or sharing.
And certainly not because a payment can purchase His favor.
But Christian generosity can be a meaningful expression of worship when it is offered freely, responsibly, and with a sincere desire to serve others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 gives us a beautiful example of believers supporting Gospel ministry through their material generosity.
But freely given support can still be a sincere offering of gratitude to God.
It can help sustain the time, effort, resources, and continued work involved in creating, developing, and sharing Gospel-centered content.
It can help us pursue the mission of reaching more people with the message that forgiveness, repentance, and transformation are found in Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into a more consistent life of biblical learning and spiritual growth.
The library's free resources remain a gift to the community, not something you must purchase to earn access to God's truth.
Those items are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way we can express appreciation to those who choose to stand alongside the ministry.
You are no less welcome.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share the Gospel matters.
Your presence in a community seeking to honor Jesus matters.
Our purpose is not to build a community where financial supporters are treated as more spiritually valuable than everyone else.
Our purpose is to keep pointing people to Jesus.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Is obedience evidence of salvation?
Scripture teaches that genuine saving faith bears fruit, and obedience is one important expression of that fruit.
Does that mean Christians should measure their worth by flawless performance?
No.
Does grace mean we can deliberately embrace sin without concern?
No.
Does every struggling believer need to live in terror that one failure has erased the work of Christ?
No.
And does a confident profession of faith make repentance and discipleship irrelevant?
Again, no.
Obedience is not the root of our salvation. Christ is our Savior, and obedience is among the fruits of a life being transformed by His grace.
The fruit matters.
But the fruit cannot replace the Savior.

And one day, when every earthly title, ministry achievement, religious reputation, and public accomplishment has faded, none of us will stand before God boasting that we were good enough to save ourselves.
Our only hope will be the mercy of God in Jesus Christ.
So follow Him.
Not to make Him die for you again.
He already gave Himself.
Not to earn a place at a table that His grace alone can provide.
But because the Savior who calls you is worthy of your trust, your love, your repentance, and your life.
When you stumble, return to Him.
When you grow proud, remember the cross.
When you become discouraged, remember the empty tomb.
When you are tempted to compromise, remember the price of your redemption.
And when religious fear whispers that you must become perfect before Jesus will receive you, remember the criminal who turned toward a dying King and heard the promise of paradise.
He had no lifetime of good works to present.
He had a Savior to trust.
And the same Jesus who received that dying man still calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him today.
You do not obey to make Jesus your Savior; you obey because the Savior who rescued you is rewriting the story sin once controlled.
